Sales 13: More on ona'ah, overcharging: waiving it knowingly, selling at cost plus a stated profit, the sales it doesn't apply to (trades, land, servants, documents), and rentals, hired workers and contractors.
Sales 14: Fair prices for food: limits on profit and on hoarding staples, a town's right to set prices, and at the end, hurting someone with words, which is worse than cheating him of money.
Sales 15: A mistake in the count, or a defect in what was sold: when the buyer can return it, what counts as a defect, and a seller who lists defects to protect himself.
Sales 16: Defects found later: seeds that don't sprout, an ox that gores or turns out treif, who pays when a hidden defect causes a loss, and food that turns out to be forbidden.
Sales 17: Selling goods of a stated quality: wheat that is worse (or better) than described, wine that turns sour, and what "fragrant" or "aged" wine has to mean.
Sales 18: No deceiving in business, toward anyone: no making old things look new, mixing produce or watering wine, and how local custom decides what a buyer must accept.
Sales 19: The seller's responsibility: telling the buyer about a dispute over the property, repaying him if it's taken away, how conditions in a deal are understood, and sales with no responsibility.
Sales 20: Disputes after a sale: a buyer who doesn't know which of five people sold to him, a storekeeper who says he was never paid, and who owns an animal born around the time of the trade.
Sales 21: Sales without exact terms: what "this heap" includes, how much land comes with a house, a burial plot, a ditch or a path, and how the boundaries in the deed decide what was sold.
Sales 22: You can't sell what doesn't exist yet or isn't yours: next year's fruit, something you haven't acquired, or something you can't touch, like a fragrance. Gifts to the Beis Hamikdash and the poor work differently.
Sales 23: Selling a field's produce but keeping the field, selling land for a set time, and buying the use of a dovecote, a beehive or trees for lumber, leaving enough to grow back.
Sales 24: Trees and the ground under them: buying three trees includes land, two do not; who owns what when land and trees are sold apart, and what a house sale includes.
Sales 25: What comes with a sale: a house with its fixtures (but not a room behind it), a courtyard, an olive press and a bathhouse, each with what belongs to it.
Sales 26: What comes with a town or a field, the paths a seller keeps to reach what he didn't sell, and the rule behind it all: follow local custom.
Sales 27: What comes with a ship, a wagon, a yoke, a donkey or a servant; why the price paid doesn't prove what was meant; and again, local custom decides.
Sales 28: Land sold by measure ("enough to sow a kor"): how far it may be over or under, and how the difference is made up.
Sales 29: Who can buy and sell: a deaf-mute, someone not of sound mind, a child (from about six, if he understands, but not land), and when a young heir may sell inherited land. A drunk man's deals stand.
Sales 30: Acquiring for someone else, sales by a servant and by a wife, and a sale made on Shabbos: forbidden, but binding.
Ownerless Property and Gifts 1: Ownerless things belong to whoever takes them: fish, birds and animals of the wild, the estate of a convert who left no heirs, and where one of his fields ends and the next begins.
Ownerless Property and Gifts 2: How ownerless land is taken: building, fencing, digging or planting with the intent to own it, and what doesn't count.
Ownerless Property and Gifts 3: How a gift is made: the recipient must take possession. Defining the gift, gifts with conditions or meant to be returned, and gifts to a servant or a married woman.
Ownerless Property and Gifts 4: Once a gift is accepted it can't be undone. Accepting a gift on someone else's behalf (even for a newborn), and disputes over whether something was given at all.
Ownerless Property and Gifts 5: A gift must be given openly: a protest made beforehand in private cancels it. Two deeds for the same field.
Ownerless Property and Gifts 6: Reading the giver's intent: everything to one son (he manages it for all) or to one's wife, a gift made on a false report that a son died, a home given at a son's wedding, and gifts to a bride when a match is called off.
Ownerless Property and Gifts 7: Shushvinus, wedding gifts meant to be returned in kind at the giver's wedding: when they can be claimed, and how much.
Ownerless Property and Gifts 8: The gifts of a person on his deathbed: who counts as one, why his words alone are enough, that they take effect only after he dies, and what happens if he recovers.
Ownerless Property and Gifts 9: More on a deathbed gift: the words that work, a recipient who refuses, changing one's mind, and a deed found after death.
Ownerless Property and Gifts 10: A dying person's instructions and admissions: "give him a maneh", "I owe him", money a father was seen hiding, and the order in which gifts are paid.
Ownerless Property and Gifts 11: Understanding a dying person's words: who "my sons" includes, two people with the same name, "a portion", "my movable property", and a request not to be eulogized.
Ownerless Property and Gifts 12: "My son shall inherit", and gifts in a chain ("to him, and after him to another"): what the first may do with them. The righteous who would not take gifts at all.
Neighbors 1: Dividing jointly owned property: when one partner can insist on dividing, what is too small to divide, and the offer "buy my share or sell me yours".
Neighbors 2: The four cubits of courtyard that belong to each house, dividing between partners and brothers, and building a dividing wall.
Neighbors 3: Rebuilding a fallen wall between neighbors, a railing for a roof, and sharing the water of one spring or river.
Neighbors 4: A loft over someone else's house: who rebuilds, and how, when they fall. Gardens one above another on a slope, and trees washed onto another's land.
Neighbors 5: Sharing a courtyard or a lane: a gatehouse, animals and mills, new windows and doors, and what the neighbors may stop.
Neighbors 6: What a city's people must share: a wall, gates, a shul and a Sefer Torah, and who pays. Which businesses neighbors may keep out; no one may stop a teacher of Torah to children.
Neighbors 7: Windows and privacy: building a wall near a neighbor's window, when a window has earned its place, and moving a window so someone can build. Refusing what costs you nothing is the way of Sedom.
Neighbors 8: Things that reach over a neighbor's yard: a ledge, a ladder, a drainpipe, a beam in his wall, and when keeping quiet lets them stay.
Neighbors 9: How far to keep things from a neighbor's wall: a cistern, a mill, an oven, a launderer's stone. An oven or a barn below a neighbor's storeroom.
Neighbors 10: Trees, threshing floors and tanneries kept away from a town. Damage that comes on its own versus "shooting arrows" into a neighbor's property; roots and branches across the line.
Neighbors 11: Dust, smell and shaking that reach a neighbor. Keeping quiet usually gives up the right to object, but never for smoke, a latrine's smell, dust or shaking.
Neighbors 12: Dividing a field fairly. Then a new topic: the neighbor's right to buy land sold next to his own, from "do what is right and good," and the sales it doesn't cover.
Neighbors 13: Ways around the neighbor's right that don't work: a "gift," a swap, a strip bought first. What the neighbor repays when he takes over, and who may use the right.
Neighbors 14: The neighbor must decide on the spot; how he loses the right; a sale below or above value; and who comes first when two want to buy. This ends Neighbors.
Agents and Partners 1: A new topic: agents. Words alone appoint one; an agent who strays from his instructions, even slightly, undoes the deal. Paying a debt through an agent, and who must swear.
Agents and Partners 2: Who may be an agent; when the other side knew he was an agent; a broker who sells below the owner's price; and an agent who claims a loss.
Agents and Partners 3: Power of attorney: when a written authorization is needed to go to court for someone, a partner who sues for everyone, and the Geonim's rule for loans, which the Rambam finds weak.
Agents and Partners 4: A new topic: partners. How a partnership is formed, how profit and loss are shared, and when a partner may end it.
Agents and Partners 5: What a partner may not do without the other: travel, sell on credit, switch goods; a loss from going his own way is his alone. Dividing without the other, and a partner's death.
Agents and Partners 6: An iska, where one person invests and the other does the work: half is a loan and half is held in trust, and the worker must be paid so it isn't interest. The Rambam disputes his teachers' formula.
Agents and Partners 7: More on iska: a large loss, losing and then gaining, one contract or two, and what the worker may and may not do with the money.
Agents and Partners 8: Raising animals or eggs for a share of the profit and how long the caretaker must keep them; sharecroppers; and brothers who keep an estate together.
Agents and Partners 9: The Sages' oath for partners and others who handle someone's property, even on a vague suspicion, and when that oath can no longer be asked.
Agents and Partners 10: Disputes between partners: who sets the oath, the claim "we already divided," and a loss or a debt that one partner says belongs to both. This ends Agents and Partners.
Slaves 1: A new topic: the Jewish servant. Who may be sold, no harsh or pointless work, and treating him as an equal: "whoever buys a Jewish servant buys himself a master."
Slaves 2: How a Jewish servant is acquired, how long he serves, illness and running away, redeeming him from a gentile, and the five ways he goes free.
Slaves 3: The servant's wife and children, a Canaanite maidservant as a wife, piercing the ear of one who wants to stay, and the generous gift when he leaves.
Slaves 4: The Jewish maidservant: a young girl sold by a father with nothing left, the six ways she goes free, and the mitzvah to marry her instead of keeping her a servant.
Slaves 5: A new topic: the Canaanite slave. How he is bought and freed, and the master who knocks out his tooth or eye, or another limb, and must free him.
Slaves 6: The document of release: handing it over through someone else, its wording, a dying master's wishes, and six ways it is like a get.
Slaves 7: A release must cut the master off completely. Freeing two slaves in one document, freeing half a slave, and someone who is half free.
Slaves 8: When a slave goes free without being released: sold to a gentile or out of Eretz Yisrael, fleeing to Eretz Yisrael, being treated as free. And a slave who won't take on the mitzvos.
Slaves 9: Who becomes a Canaanite slave, freeing one only for a mitzvah, and the book's last words: the law allows hard work, but the Jewish way is mercy.
Hiring 1: The Torah's four watchmen (unpaid, borrower, paid, renter) and their three laws. When the owner also works for him, negligence at the start, and passing the article to another watchman.
Hiring 2: What the watchmen's laws cover: movable property, not consecrated, of a Jew. Land, slaves and notes; women and minors; when the watch begins; agreements to take on more or less, and disputes about them.
Hiring 3: Losses beyond the watchman's control: proving them, a porter's broken jug, a shepherd and wolves, calling for help, and leaving the herd.
Hiring 4: Using a rented animal differently from what was agreed: another route, another job, another load, another rider, extra weight, and what a rider may take along.
Hiring 5: When a rented animal, ship or house is lost: was a particular one rented, or just "an animal"? Leaving a ship midway, subletting, and a rented house that falls.
Hiring 6: Renting a home: what comes with it, what the owner must fix, and how much notice each side gives before it ends, even when rents rise or the house is sold.
Hiring 7: Conditions in a rental, a leap year in a year's lease, "I paid" against "you didn't," an undated contract, an orchard that dries up, and produce left on someone's land.
Hiring 8: Renting a field for a fixed rent or for a share of the crop: what may be sown, a spring that fails, locusts and drought, weeding, and switching crops.
Hiring 9: Hiring workers: local custom on hours and pay, hiring through an agent, work that stops (the king's service, a river that dries up), finishing early, and what a worker finds.
Hiring 10: Who is a paid watchman: a lender holding security, two people who watch for each other, and every craftsman; a craftsman who ruins what he was given.
Hiring 11: The mitzvah to pay a worker on time, for his life depends on it; when it applies, hiring through an agent, and settling disputes over wages.
Hiring 12: A worker's right to eat from the produce he works with: which work, which produce, how much, and not taking it home to his family.
Hiring 13: Do not muzzle an ox while it threshes. And the book's closing: the employer may not cheat the worker, and the worker must work honestly with all his strength, as Yaakov did.
Borrowing and Deposit 1: A borrower pays even for accidents. An animal that dies while working, feeding it, how long he may keep what he borrowed, and what he may use it for.
Borrowing and Deposit 2: "If its owner was with it": when the owner is working for the borrower, he doesn't pay. Who counts as working with him, and husbands, wives and partners.
Borrowing and Deposit 3: Sending a borrowed cow: when the borrower's responsibility begins, disputes over how it died, and cows borrowed for half a day and rented for half.
Borrowing and Deposit 4: The unpaid watchman: his oath, and what counts as guarding properly. Money must be buried or hidden; leaving a deposit with his wife and household.
Borrowing and Deposit 5: Money for charity, handing a deposit to robbers, two depositors who disagree, and mixing someone's produce with your own.
